If you have ever bolted tenacity onto an OpenAI client and wondered why your outage cascade got worse, this file is the missing syllabus.

Finally, the strategy dispatch shows how to make a 16,000-line class extensible without chaos. RoutingStrategy in litellm/types/router.py at line 1157 names exactly four built-in picks - least-busy, latency-based-routing, cost-based-routing, and usage-based-routing-v2 - with simple-shuffle as the default at line 139, and _select_deployment_async at 2164 is a plain match statement over those names at 2182-2215. New strategies register through routing_strategy_init at 1809, which builds a selector object and binds it to the Router. The lesson generalizes: enumerate the decisions you actually make, give each a tiny stateful module, and keep the dispatcher dumb. Teams that adopt LiteLLM behind Open WebUI or their own agents get this machinery for free; teams that hand-roll a gateway usually reimplement only the retry half and wonder why latency silently doubles during traffic spikes. And because every hook flows through CustomLogger - 1,137 lines of documented callbacks - wiring observability like Langfuse is a config entry, not a fork.

Detail: the proxy lifecycle builds the Router at startup; auth and budget gates run per request; the retry loop alternates between healthy-set filtering, strategy selection, cooldown writes, and single attempts through the provider bridge.

Start at the gateway, because everything else inherits its globals. proxy_startup_event at line 1399 declares sixteen module-level globals at 1400-1415 - prisma_client, master_key, llm_router, store_model_in_db among them - a deliberate acknowledgment that the proxy is one long-lived process per worker. It marks stale Prometheus multiprocess directories dead at 1424-1426, then runs any LITELLM_WORKER_STARTUP_HOOKS entries at 1429-1447, importing each “module.path:function_name” spec dynamically so operators can inject startup behavior without patching the image. The chat route at 12710 is thin by design: it reads the body, copies user_id, team_id, org_id, and agent_id from the authenticated key into the metadata dict at 12742-12757, and calls base_process_llm_request with route_type “acompletion” at 12761-12765. Everything that looks like business logic lives in the 21k-line file’s other 21k lines, which is exactly why the Router’s separateness matters - the same Router object serves the proxy, the SDK, and the CLI.

The selection moment deserves a slow-motion replay. After async_function_with_retries fetches the healthy list, _select_deployment_async at 2164 asks the strategy selector for a deployment, with simple-shuffle explicitly noted in the docstring at 2175-2178 as bypassing the selector machinery. For latency-based-routing, the case at 2206-2213 forwards request_kwargs, because only the caller knows whether this request streams - and that flag flips the handler to TTFT percentiles at 451-456, a detail that separates p95 prompt-processing pain from p95 time-to-first-word pain in chat UIs. The TPM/RPM guards at 475-478 reject deployments whose budgets the request would blow through, using the rpm and tpm fields any model_list entry may declare at 440-445. Then the buffer logic at 486-498 does something quietly wise: it sorts candidates by latency, keeps everything within lowest_latency_buffer of the best, and picks randomly among them - spreading load across near-equal deployments instead of hammering one winner into its own budget.

Failure handling is the second half of the same loop. When make_call at 8743 raises, the exception handler at 8573 re-enters the loop after three bookkeeping calls: _set_deployment_num_retries_on_exception at 4425 copies the deployment’s declared patience onto the error, failed-deployment stamping at 4444-4474 marks which model_info id failed so retries can skip it, and should-fail checks consult the allowed_fails counters configured back at init 1405. Cooldowns land in cooldown_cache.py - 237 lines that wrap either an in-memory TTL structure or Redis, which is what makes the whole scheme work across the proxy’s horizontal replicas. When an entire model group is exhausted, async_function_with_fallbacks at 8402 walks the configured fallback list, carrying partial usage forward so billing stays honest across the switch - the hidden-params plumbing at 3250-3282 exists precisely so a retried stream can adopt the previous attempt’s token counts.

The bridge and the bill close the tour. main.py’s completion at 5328 is where “100+ providers” becomes real: a giant dispatch by model prefix into per-provider implementations, each normalizing errors back into LiteLLM’s own exception taxonomy so the Router’s cooldown logic can treat a Bedrock ThrottlingException and an OpenAI 429 identically. cost_per_token at cost_calculator.py line 405 reads the model_prices_and_context_window.json registry that ships at the repo root - one JSON file, thousands of models, input and output rates per token - and completion_cost at 1419 assembles the final number that the proxy writes to spend logs per key, team, and user. That registry, updated by bot PRs almost daily, is the quiet moat of the project: routing, retries, and cooldowns are ideas, but knowing what a Llama 4 Maverick call costs on six clouds is data, and data compounds.

From Install to a Balanced Gateway

The README’s quickstart gets a two-deployment gateway balancing with one config (commands abridged):

pip install 'litellm[proxy]'
export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-1234
# config.yaml: two model_list entries sharing model_name "gpt-4o",
# one openai/, one azure/, plus:
#   router_settings:
#     routing_strategy: latency-based-routing
#     allowed_fails: 3
litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \
  -d '{"model": "gpt-4o", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}'

Both entries answer to the same public name; the Router picks per request, and /health or the cooldown debug endpoint shows which deployment is currently in timeout.

Honest limits: the Router is big because the problem is big, but the size is real - 16,046 lines with streaming fallback edges (the FallbackAwareAnthropicMessagesStream at 955 exists because mid-stream provider deaths are genuinely hard), and you should not expect to internalize it in an afternoon; the in-memory cooldown and usage caches are per-process until you attach Redis, so a single-replica deployment gets weaker guarantees than the diagrams imply; strategy quality depends on honest logging, and silent callback failures degrade routing to shuffle without errors; budget limiter enforcement (941 lines in budget_limiter.py) checks at request time, not mid-stream, so one 100k-token runaway can still overshoot a TPM cap; and the Apache 2.0 license covers the core, with several enterprise features clearly fenced off in the enterprise directory.
entry.summary: A source tour of the LiteLLM Router: latency and least-busy strategy selectors, the cooldown cache, the retry and fallback layers, and the 21,000-line FastAPI proxy that fronts 100+ LLM providers.

entry.title: 100+ Models, One Command - Inside hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory
entry.content:
Where axolotl bets on one exhaustive YAML schema, LLaMA-Factory bets on breadth: one CLI that fine-tunes over a hundred model families, one data loader that speaks every open dataset format, and one stage dispatcher that walks from continuous pretraining through supervised fine-tuning into reward modeling, PPO, DPO, and KTO. The project behind the widely cited “Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models” paper has become the default answer to “how do I fine-tune X” for a whole generation of practitioners, and it ships a Gradio web UI so the entire journey runs from a browser. Apache-2.0 licensed, it packs its power into a surprisingly compact src tree of about 180 Python files - most of the surface area lives in a handful of genuinely enormous modules.

Those big modules are the story. A 2686-line template file encodes every supported chat format as data; a 3502-line multimodal plugin file teaches every vision-language family how to emit training rows; a 978-line trainer utilities file carries the callbacks and metrics every stage shares. Reading the repo is really reading three or four epic files plus a lattice of small workflow scripts that glue them together. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI routes to a stage dispatcher; argument parsing, the template registry, and dataset processing feed model loading and the workflows; a chat facade serves the result.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli.py is a 31-line console entry that forwards every subcommand to the launcher.
  • launcher.py at 185 lines routes train, chat, api, export, webui, and eval to their implementations.
  • hparams/parser.py defines get_train_args at line 395, fusing five argument families into one validated tuple.
  • train/tuner.py exposes run_exp at line 163 with the stage dispatch at line 69.
  • data/loader.py loads and merges datasets via get_dataset at line 276 with caching at line 229.
  • data/template.py is the template registry: register_template at line 681 defines every supported chat format.
  • data/processor/supervised.py tokenizes rows in SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51.
  • model/loader.py builds the model while chat/chat_model.py serves it afterwards.

Why You Need This

Every fine-tuning tool solves the same four problems - arguments, data, model prep, training loop - and comparing implementations is the fastest way to understand the trade space. Where the axolotl tour showed a pydantic schema validating one giant YAML, LLaMA-Factory shows the Hugging Face idiom: five dataclass families (model, data, training, finetuning, generating) parsed from CLI or dict and cross-verified in _verify_model_args at line 227 of the parser. Neither is wrong; seeing both teaches you what a config system must guarantee regardless of style. The same comparison holds for adapters - this repo’s model/adapter.py implements full, freeze, and LoRA tuning side by side, next to the PEFT internals we covered in the peft tour.

The template registry deserves particular attention because it quietly carries the entire “100+ models” claim. A chat model fine-tune is useless if the prompt format does not match the pretrained format, and this file turns that compatibility problem into data: each register_template call declares system messages, user and assistant wrappers, stop tokens, and tool-call encodings for one family. New model support lands as a few lines of registration rather than a fork of the trainer - which is exactly why the README’s day-0 support table keeps filling in. If you maintain any chat-adjacent system, this is the most complete public catalog of what varies between chat formats.

Multimodal support is the other eye-opener. The data/mm_plugin.py file gives every vision-language family - LLaVA, Gemma 3, InternVL, Kimi-VL and more - a plugin that converts raw rows into the exact interleave of text and image/video tokens that family’s model class expects, including pixel-value preprocessing and image token splicing. Rather than one generic VLM loader, the repo embraces per-family reality. And when the current architecture finally hits its limits, the v1 subtree shows the rewrite: a cleaner engine split (data_engine, model_engine, base_trainer) with its own plugin system - worth reading as a case study in how projects migrate themselves.

Detailed view: entry and dispatch, argument families, the data machinery with templates and multimodal plugins, model preparation, the six stage trainers, and the inference surface.

Follow one stage end to end. llamafactory-cli train lands in launcher.py, which calls run_exp at line 163 of train/tuner.py; read_args at line 112 of hparams/parser.py accepts either a dict or command-line tokens, and get_train_args at line 395 returns the five-class tuple after _verify_model_args at line 227 rejects contradictions like a missing template. The _training_function at line 69 then dispatches: stage sft goes to run_sft at line 41 of train/sft/workflow.py, while pt, rm, ppo, dpo, and kto each have a sibling workflow - and lines 92 through 136 show optional detours into hyper-parallel, Megatron-Bridge, and Megatron-core backends when those packages are installed.

The data path inside run_sft is the loader at work. data/loader.py merges every named dataset at line 164, converts rows via data/converter.py (alpaca, sharegpt, openai formats), resolves the chat template through get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819 of data/template.py, and hands rows to the processors: SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51 of data/processor/supervised.py builds input_ids with labels masked outside responses, its packed subclass at line 146 concatenates sequences with position-id resets, and the PairwiseDatasetProcessor at line 30 of data/processor/pairwise.py produces the chosen/rejected pairs that DPO and reward stages consume. Collators from data/collator.py finish the batches.

Model preparation is the patcher’s show. model/loader.py picks quantization through model/model_utils/quantization.py - AQLM, AWQ, GPTQ, HQQ, EETQ, and bitsandbytes variants - then model/patcher.py applies patch_config at line 365 (rope scaling, attention impl, flash-attn selection), patch_model at line 437 (longlora shift attention, packed attention, MoE and vision fixes), and unsloth support from model/model_utils/unsloth.py when requested. init_adapter at line 317 of model/adapter.py then branches: full tuning at line 38, freeze tuning at line 57, and _setup_lora_tuning at line 147 covering LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, and LoftQ variants. The workflow finishes by instantiating CustomSeq2SeqTrainer at line 47 of train/sft/trainer.py with metrics from train/trainer_utils.py.

The serving half closes the loop. ChatModel at line 39 of chat/chat_model.py wraps three engines - hf, vLLM (VllmEngine at line 46 of chat/vllm_engine.py), and sglang - behind one astream_chat interface; api/app.py exposes it as an OpenAI-compatible server; and the LLaMA Board web UI’s webui/runner.py submits training jobs straight into the same run_exp entry, so GUI and CLI are one system. Evaluation through eval/evaluator.py scores MMLU-style benchmarks with the same template machinery.

Two registries make the 100-model claim hold up. The template registry in data/template.py is a plain dict called TEMPLATES at line 678, filled by register_template at line 681 and consulted by get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819; the base Template class at line 41 carries specializations like Llama2Template at line 454 for the older Llama chat format, and ReasoningTemplate at line 524 with its Qwen38ReasoningTemplate subclass at line 593 for models that emit thinking traces before answers. Multimodal support follows the same shape in mm_plugin.py, a 3,502-line module whose BasePlugin at line 421 defines the default vision interface and whose per-family subclasses - Gemma3Plugin at line 876, InternVLPlugin at line 1180, KimiVLPlugin at line 1330, and LlavaPlugin at line 1429 - override how images and videos expand into placeholder tokens, how processor outputs are cached, and how the collator stitches visual features into the sequence. Adding a new model family usually means registering one template and one plugin instead of touching the trainer at all.

The alignment stages get their own trainers with minimal duplication. CustomDPOTrainer at line 44 of train/dpo/trainer.py extends the TRL DPOTrainer and overrides concatenated_forward at line 219 to route preference batches through the repo’s own collators and mm plugin, while CustomPPOTrainer at line 64 of train/ppo/trainer.py inherits from both PPOTrainer and Trainer to blend rollout generation with the standard optimization step. Cross-cutting behavior lands in callbacks rather than trainer edits: LogCallback at line 174 of train/callbacks.py appends each stage’s timing and loss to the trainer_log.jsonl you find in every output directory, PissaConvertCallback at line 132 swaps PiSSA adapters between their init and training representations, ReporterCallback at line 433 writes the training report when a run ends, and ModuleProfilerCallback at line 491 measures per-module memory so you can spot which layers are worth offloading or quantizing. When one node is not enough, run_exp checks ray_args.use_ray and re-enters itself through Ray, with the placement-group helpers in trainer_utils.py - get_placement_group, get_ray_head_node_ip, sort_placement_group_by_node_ip - pinning workers across the cluster, so the same YAML scales from a single GPU to a multi-node job without edits.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s zero-code loop:

uv run llamafactory-cli webui
llamafactory-cli train examples/train_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli chat examples/inference/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli export examples/merge_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml

Or programmatically, one dict instead of YAML:

from llamafactory.train.tuner import run_exp

run_exp(args={
    "stage": "sft",
    "model_name_or_path": "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    "template": "qwen3",
    "dataset": "alpaca_en_demo",
    "finetuning_type": "lora",
    "output_dir": "qwen3-lora-out",
})

Swap stage to dpo with a pairwise dataset and the same entry runs preference tuning; point infer_backend at vllm and the same chat model serves hundreds of concurrent requests.

Honest limits: the breadth comes with weight - the giant template, mm_plugin, and trainer_utils files are dense and occasionally duplicate logic across stage trainers, so tracing one behavior can mean reading three files. The WebUI covers the happy path well but exotic combinations still want the CLI. And because so much support is template registration plus small patches, per-model quirks sometimes surface only in that model’s issue tracker, not the docs.
entry.summary: A source tour of LLaMA-Factory, the unified fine-tuning factory: a 2686-line chat template registry, multimodal plugins, stage dispatch from pretraining to PPO, and a v1 engine rewrite.

entry.title: The Memory Core - Inside ggml-org/llama.cpp’s KV Cache Redesign

link.title: The Memory Core - Inside ggml-org/llama.cpp’s KV Cache Redesign

entry.content:
The most consequential project in local inference has quietly moved house - the repository now lives as ggml-org/llama.cpp - and while the logo stayed, the internals have been rebuilt around an abstraction that barely existed when this series first toured the codebase: a polymorphic memory layer. Where older versions wired a single KV cache directly into llama_context, the current master defines llama_memory_i in src/llama-memory.h and implements it five ways - the classic attention cache, a dual sliding-window cache, recurrent state cells, a hybrid of the two, and more - so that transformer models, Mamba-style models, and everything in between flow through one decode loop. This second tour of the project skips what we covered before and goes straight for the redesign: the memory interface, the find-slot machinery that decides whether your prompt fits, and the one-shot optimization retry that stands between you and an error.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the public API feeds a decode loop that initializes batches, asks a polymorphic memory module for context, and processes ubatches through the graph; the KV cache anchors five implementations; failures trigger a one-shot optimization retry; the modular server drives it all from a task queue.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • src/llama.cpp is now just 621 lines of C API exports - the real engine lives in llama-context.cpp, 4,719 lines, whose decode at line 1821 is the single path every model takes.
  • llama_context::decode at line 1821 initializes the batch allocator at 1879, applies pending memory shifts at 1920, and enters a loop asking the memory module for a context via init_batch at 1925.
  • src/llama-batch.cpp, 1,493 lines, is the traffic splitter: llama_batch_allocr::init at line 28 validates input, then split_simple at 585, split_equal at 619, and split_seq at 790 carve one user batch into ubatches the graph can chew.
  • src/llama-memory.h is the new contract: init_batch at line 89, init_full at 95, init_update at 99, plus a seq_* family at 111-118 that gives every backend the same branching, copying, and position-shift vocabulary.
  • src/llama-kv-cache.cpp, 2,962 lines, is the reference implementation: prepare at line 771 walks ubatches, find_slot at 918 hunts for contiguous space, and apply_ubatch at 1117 commits the choice.
  • src/llama-kv-cache-iswa.cpp holds the SWA dual cache in 355 lines - a full cache for sinks and a sliding one for the rest - while llama-memory-hybrid.cpp, 283 lines, pairs attention and recurrent modules for Jamba-style architectures, and llama-memory-recurrent.cpp, 1,386 lines, keeps fixed-size state for Mamba-family models.
  • src/llama-sampler.cpp, 4,391 lines, chains token filters around one softmax at line 293: greedy at 1113, dist at 1405, top_k at 1525, top_p at 1725, min_p at 1888, typical at 2000, temp at 2110, xtc at 2422, grammar at 2831, and dry at 3645.
  • tools/server/server-queue.cpp, 621 lines, shows how far the server has modularized: post at line 28, deferred tasks at 76, and worker_loop at 163 - with a 6,313-line server-context.cpp, a 1,904-line server-task.cpp, and an MCP integration at server-mcp.cpp (799 lines) behind a main.cpp of just 5 lines.

Why You Need This

The polymorphic memory layer is the answer to a question this series keeps circling: how does one C++ codebase serve both a transformer and a state-space model without forking? The old answer was if-statements scattered through the context; the new answer is that llama_context holds a single llama_memory_i pointer and speaks only the interface - init_batch to start, seq_rm and seq_cp to edit, state_write at line 126 of the header to snapshot. When you run a Mamba model, the pointer points at llama-memory-recurrent.cpp; a hybrid Jamba architecture gets the 283-line coordinator; a Llama-family model gets the classic cache. Compare this with how vLLM bolted sliding-window support onto its paged allocator, or how ollama embeds an older llama.cpp and inherits whatever the snapshot had - reading the interface here shows what a clean second-architecture migration looks like when it is finished.

The find-slot machinery is worth its own visit because it is the heart of multi-sequence serving. find_slot at line 918 searches the cell grid for room for a ubatch - contiguity per sequence, headroom across the batch - and prepare at 771 runs it ahead of compute so failure is cheap. When preparation fails, decode’s status switch at 1930-1962 hits LLAMA_MEMORY_STATUS_FAILED_PREPARE and does exactly one thing: memory_update(true) at 1945, which shifts cache contents and optimizes fragmentation, then retries the same batch once - the debug line at 1946 says “retrying batch size after cache optimization,” and a second failure returns 1 at 1954. One retry, not a loop: the design accepts that a genuinely full context must fail loudly rather than thrash. Every LLM server reinvents this dance - llamafile sidesteps it with fixed allocations, TGI leans on its router’s queue - and seeing the minimal correct version in 30 lines is the best tutorial available.

Finally, the sampler file is a museum of decoding folklore, and the current layout teaches the chain-of-responsibility pattern with unusual clarity. Every filter - top_k, top_p, min_p, typical, temp, xtc, dry - is a tiny struct that mutates a token array in place, all funneling through the shared softmax at line 293, and the grammar sampler at 2831 simply zeroes out logits that the grammar forbids. The newest twist is backend sampling: decode opens a per-batch sampling transaction at 1974-1976 with llama_sampler_backend_begin, pushing the chain onto the GPU so the CPU never sees intermediate distributions - the same direction whisper.cpp took for its own hot loops. The sibling project comparison is not decorative: both live under the ggml umbrella, share ggml’s backend abstraction, and demonstrate how far a dependency-free C/C++ stack can stretch.

Detail: the decode loop wires batch splitting, memory preparation, graph building, and backend sampling; five memory backends share one sequence-operations vocabulary; the modular server queues tasks into the same C API.

The decode loop repays a full read. After the allocator initializes at 1879, decode counts outputs per sequence at 1853-1877 and rejects batches that exceed the backend-sampling output cap - a new constraint that did not exist when sampling lived on the CPU. The memory handoff at 1925 returns a llama_memory_context_ptr, a scoped object whose get_status() at 1930 tells the loop whether preparation succeeded; the one-shot optimize path lives at 1940-1955. Per ubatch, process_ubatch at line 1507 builds the graph via llama-graph.cpp (4,265 lines), computes, and on failure rolls back just the positions of that ubatch at 2004-2015 - an undo log in twelve lines. output_reorder at 2422 then untangles per-sequence outputs into batch order, and synchronize at 871 is the barrier callers hit before reading logits. The legacy llama_batch wrappers at 4601-4606 adapt the old public API onto llama_batch_ext, so years of downstream code keep compiling - a compatibility discipline worth copying in any long-lived library.

The KV cache itself is a small database, and the seq_* operations are its CRUD API. seq_rm at line 404 removes position ranges, seq_cp at 473 duplicates a sequence - the operation behind speculative decoding’s draft trees - seq_keep at 565 prunes everything else, and seq_add at 592 shifts positions, which is the mechanism behind context shifting when a conversation outgrows its window. prepare at 771 and find_slot at 918 enforce the invariants: cells for a ubatch must be contiguous per sequence, and get_can_shift at 1210 declares whether a backend can slide at all (recurrent state cannot; attention caches can). set_input_kq_mask at 1761 then writes the attention mask that encodes every one of those decisions into the graph - the last place where sequence bookkeeping becomes tensor data. The iswa variant at 355 lines runs two caches side by side because sliding-window layers and full-attention layers in the same model (Gemma-style interleaving) need different eviction horizons, and the hybrid coordinator delegates per layer type.

The server rewrite is the quiet headline of this tour. main.cpp is five lines; server.cpp holds 562; the actual behavior is spread across eighteen focused modules. server-queue.cpp posts tasks at line 28, defers continuation-style tasks at 76, and pops them when a slot frees at 90, while worker_loop at 163 drains the queue - a producer-consumer design that replaced the old monolithic loop. server-context.cpp (6,313 lines) owns inference slots and task execution, server-task.cpp (1,904 lines) defines the task types and result marshaling, server-mcp.cpp (799 lines) wires Model Context Protocol tool calling into completions, and the 5-line main is the reviewability payoff: a new contributor reads one module, not one monster. The same C API the CLI and bindings call is all the server uses, which keeps the library honest - if the server cannot do it through the public interface, users cannot either.

The model side stays the least changed. llama-model.cpp (3,985 lines) and the loader build tensor graphs per architecture at load time, llama-grammar.cpp (1,530 lines) implements the GBNF engine that the grammar sampler consults, and the whole stack sits on ggml’s backend abstraction - CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL - so the memory layer above never learns which hardware is underneath. That layering, interface over implementation over hardware, is the durable lesson of this codebase: the parts that were refactored (memory, server) are exactly the parts that had leaked across layers, and the parts left alone were already clean.

From Install to a Cached Sequence

Building and driving the server still takes three commands (abridged):

cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j
./build/bin/llama-server -m models/qwen2.5-7b-q4_k_m.gguf --ctx-size 8192 --port 8080
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
# observe the cache at work:
curl http://localhost:8080/props | head   # default_generation_settings, slots

Prompt caching is automatic: a follow-up request sharing the conversation prefix finds its cells via find_slot and computes only the new tokens - watch the timings field report n_prompt_tokens_processed shrinking to single digits.

Honest limits: the memory redesign is C++17 through and through, and the interface’s power comes with pointer juggling that demands care from embedders; the one-shot optimization retry means pathological fragmentation patterns can still fail a batch that a second retry would fit; recurrent memory keeps fixed-size state, so long-context claims for Mamba-family models depend on that state size, not on cache eviction; backend sampling caps outputs per sequence (enforced at decode 1853-1877), which unusual batch shapes can hit unexpectedly; the server’s 6,313-line context module is a lot of state in one file despite the modularization; and the org move to ggml-org means old clone URLs redirect - pin your remotes and your known_hosts.
entry.summary: A second source tour of llama.cpp, now under ggml-org: the unified llama_memory interface, the KV cache find-slot machinery, SWA and hybrid and recurrent backends, batch splitting, the decode retry loop, and the modularized task-queue server.

entry.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

link.title: The Ruler Every LLM Paper Trusts - Inside EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness

entry.content:
Every benchmark number you have seen attached to an open model - MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, ARC, TruthfulQA - has a decent chance of having been produced by this repository. EleutherAI’s Language Model Evaluation Harness is the framework behind the Open LLM Leaderboard and hundreds of papers, and its power comes from an architecture that treats evaluation as data: every task is a YAML file describing prompts, document formats, and metrics, and the framework’s job is to turn any language model into a scoring function against those files. Release 0.4.14 under the MIT license ships with 221 task directories under lm_eval/tasks, each holding configs that expand into hundreds of benchmark subtasks and variants.

What makes the source worth reading is that it is a masterclass in interface design under constraint. The whole system communicates through two verbs - loglikelihood and generate_until - so anything that can answer those two requests becomes an evaluable model, from a Hugging Face checkpoint to a vLLM engine to a commercial API to a llama.cpp GGUF file. Around that spine sits a task system powerful enough to encode fewshot selection, answer extraction, and metric aggregation as declarative config, plus a plugin registry that keeps 30 model backends from tangling the core. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI drives the evaluator, which pulls tasks from the manager and requests from the model abstraction; answers flow through filters into aggregation and result logging.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • lm_eval/_cli/run.py is the 518-line entry that parses CLI flags into a simple_evaluate call.
  • lm_eval/evaluator.py holds the two public functions: simple_evaluate at line 55 and the core evaluate loop at line 429 of its 714 lines.
  • lm_eval/tasks/manager.py defines TaskManager at line 37, the indexer that turns task names into config-loaded classes.
  • lm_eval/api/task.py is the 1808-line heart: Task at line 64, ConfigurableTask at line 618.
  • lm_eval/api/model.py declares the LM interface at line 25 with TemplateLM at line 356 and CachingLM at line 275.
  • lm_eval/models/huggingface.py is the reference backend, HFLM at line 62 of 1782 lines.
  • lm_eval/api/filter.py pairs the Filter contract at line 8 with FilterEnsemble at line 34, fed by regex extractors in filters/extraction.py.
  • lm_eval/loggers/evaluation_tracker.py persists everything through EvaluationTracker at line 123.

Why You Need This

If you have followed the fine-tuning tours here - LLaMA-Factory, axolotl, unsloth - you have watched the training side of the loop. The harness is the other half: the tool that tells you whether a model got better. Reading it teaches you what benchmark numbers actually measure, because every step that could silently change a score is explicit: which prompt template was used, how many fewshot examples were sampled and by what rule, how the raw generation was cut down to an answer, and which aggregation produced the table cell. Reproducibility is not a slogan here; it is enforced by config files checked into the repo.

The backend abstraction is the lesson most applicable elsewhere. Anything implementing loglikelihood and generate_until plugs in - and the catalog shows the range: HFLM for transformers checkpoints with quantization support, VLLM for batched inference throughput, TemplateAPI for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Megatron for very large models, plus GGUF, ONNX, and Neuron variants. The same interface idea powers ctranslate2 and onnxruntime in serving, and seeing it applied to evaluation makes a strong argument for tiny, honest interfaces over framework lock-in.

The task system deserves study if you ever design datasets or leaderboards. ConfigurableTask turns a YAML file into prompt construction, target extraction, and metric selection, while the filter ensemble composes regex extraction, whitespace trimming, and majority-vote selection into the answer stage. The metric library covers everything from exact match and F1 to BLEU, chrF, perplexity, and bits-per-byte, with aggregation declared per task so nothing is hard-coded. Once you have seen how much behavior fits in declarative config, you will never hard-code an eval script again.

Detailed view: CLI entry, the evaluation core, the task API with metrics and samplers, the backend family registered against the LM interface, task definition loading, filters, and logging with caching.

The main flow starts at simple_evaluate at line 55 of evaluator.py, which resolves the model through get_model at line 613 of api/registry.py, builds the task list through a TaskManager constructed in tasks/manager.py, applies decontamination and limits, and then hands everything to evaluate at line 429 - the loop that batches requests per task, sorts them across tasks for throughput, calls the model, and routes outputs through filters and aggregation. The supporting math lands in evaluator_utils.py: get_sample_size at line 49, the aggregation accumulator at line 99, group-aware rollups through aggregate_groups at line 301, and result shaping in _process_results at line 375 of its 540 lines.

The registry is the hinge of the whole design. Registry at line 270 of api/registry.py is a generic plugin container fed by load_plugins at line 189 and import_plugins at line 246; register_model at line 587 lets any backend class join the catalog by name, DEFAULT_METRIC_REGISTRY at line 571 maps task output types to default metrics, and get_model at line 613 is the single factory call the evaluator makes. This is why the models directory can hold thirty backends - anthropic, openai_completions, textsynth, sglang, trtllm, neuron, watsonx - without the core importing any of them.

The breadth of that directory repays a skim. HFMultimodalLM at line 30 of models/hf_vlms.py extends HFLM across its 750 lines for vision-language checkpoints; MambaLMWrapper at line 10 of models/mamba_lm.py shows a state-space model joining the club through the same base class in just 164 lines; GGUFLM at line 24 of models/gguf.py implements the LM interface directly to talk to llama.cpp; and TRTLLM at line 37 of models/trtllm_causallms.py covers TensorRT-LLM deployments in 631 lines. Even audio generation gets a slot through hf_audiolm.py, and the thinness of the smaller wrappers is the point - the easier a backend is to write, the better the interface is doing its job.

Every backend implements the same small interface from api/model.py: LM at line 25 declares loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling, and generate_until; TemplateLM at line 356 implements the shared tokenization glue for models that expose token access; CachingLM at line 275 wraps any backend with a sqlite cache keyed by hash_args at line 255, so repeated runs replay identical requests for free. The reference implementation, HFLM at line 62 of models/huggingface.py, handles device placement, batching, PEFT adapters, and quantized checkpoints across its 1782 lines; VLLM at line 59 of models/vllm_causallms.py swaps throughput into the same contract; and TemplateAPI at line 105 of models/api_models.py does the same for remote endpoints, with shared helpers like handle_stop_sequences at line 641 of models/utils.py keeping behavior aligned.

The task layer is where YAML becomes evaluation. TaskManager at line 37 indexes every task config, tasks/_yaml_loader.py loads them with include-resolution and safe function imports through load_yaml at line 164, and tasks/_factory.py builds concrete tasks through TaskFactory at line 25. The resulting ConfigurableTask at line 618 of api/task.py is an engine of over a thousand lines that constructs fewshot contexts through ContextSampler at line 17 of api/samplers.py (with FirstNSampler, BalancedSampler at line 117, and ManualSampler variants), builds Instance requests from api/instance.py, scores outputs with the metric functions in api/metrics.py - mean at line 35, perplexity at line 47, f1_score at line 62, bleu at line 102 - and specializes into MultipleChoiceTask at line 1688 and PerplexityTask at line 1735 for the two classic evaluation shapes. Groups compose tasks hierarchically through Group at line 34 of api/group.py and ConfigurableGroup at line 346.

Answer extraction gets its own layer because raw generations rarely match gold strings directly. Filter at line 8 of api/filter.py is the contract and FilterEnsemble at line 34 chains several; filters/extraction.py provides RegexFilter at line 16, a POS-aware filter at line 66, WhitespaceFilter at line 110, and MultiChoiceRegexFilter at line 123 for multiple-choice formats, while filters/selection.py implements majority voting over sampled generations. Results finally flow through the logging stack: GeneralConfigTracker at line 38 and EvaluationTracker at line 123 of loggers/evaluation_tracker.py write samples, configs, and tables to disk or the Hub, loggers/wandb_logger.py streams the same to experiment dashboards, and the 88 lines of caching/cache.py back the request cache that makes reruns nearly instant. Even discovery is a first-class feature - lm_eval/_cli/ls.py powers lm-eval ls tasks and ls models against the same index the runner consumes.

From Install to a Benchmark Table

Install with the backends you need, then evaluate:

pip install "lm_eval[hf,vllm]"
lm_eval --model hf \
    --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b \
    --tasks hellaswag,arc_easy \
    --device cuda:0 --batch_size 8

The same run from Python:

import lm_eval

results = lm_eval.simple_evaluate(
    model="hf",
    model_args="pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-1.4b",
    tasks=["hellaswag", "arc_easy"],
    num_fewshot=0,
)
print(results["results"])

Both paths return per-task metric tables plus samples you can inspect, and the tracker writes them to JSON for later comparison.

Honest limits: benchmark scores are proxies, and the harness makes prompt and extraction choices visible but cannot make them neutral; a few backend integrations lag the latest upstream releases; and running 221 task groups naively costs real money and compute, so sane usage starts with limit and a hand-picked task list. The value of the source is that none of these limits are hidden - every choice is a line you can read.
entry.summary: A source tour of the EleutherAI evaluation harness: one YAML-driven ConfigurableTask format, a plugin registry of model backends from Hugging Face to vLLM to llama.cpp, fewshot samplers, regex answer filters, and the aggregation machinery behind benchmark tables.
